title: LiverDoc vs Ayurveda Debate | Dr Cyriac Abby Philips #ayurveda #debate #abbyphilips
description:
***The Complete video of the recent Debate between Vaidya Vasundhara Sadhineni and Dr Cyriac Abby Philips can be viewed here - https://youtube.com/live/z1_zou2Vil0***

On 16 September 2023, Twitter Spaces lit up when Ayurveda practitioner Omkar Kulkarni and hepatologist Dr. Cyriac Abby Philips (TheLiverDoc) clashed over one of the biggest questions in Indian health: Should Ayurveda and modern medicine be integrated, or is that mixing faith with fantasy?

In this debate:

Omkar Kulkarni defends Ayurveda, tradition, and ancient practices, arguing for the value of holistic healing, tradition, and local cultural knowledge.

Dr. Cyriac Abby Philips pushes back with science: demanding clinical proof, evidence from randomized controlled trials, safety data (especially liver safety), and warning about herbal remedies that may cause harm.

They also discuss herb-induced liver injury (HILI), regulation of herbal medicines, standards of safety and evidence, and whether “integrative medicine” is just a polite name for pseudoscience.

Dr. Philips is well known for his activism against harmful claims in alternative medicine, especially in liver damage cases. He has flagged serious risks from Tinospora cordifolia (Giloy) and other herbal immune boosters causing acute and autoimmune-type hepatitis in multiple patients. 

Omkar Kulkarni has defended the traditional use of such herbs, citing historical usage and Ayurvedic theory (though critics say that history ≠ safety/effectiveness).

This isn’t a clean “science vs tradition” story. It’s about proof vs belief, regulation vs freedom, harm vs hope, and whether integrating Ayurveda into mainstream healthcare dilutes scientific rigour—or can enhance accessibility and cultural relevance.

You’re asking for large RCTs — fair. But then be consistent and acknowledge where they already exist.

• Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera):
Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials show significant reduction in stress and serum cortisol.
(Chandrasekhar et al., Indian J Psychol Med, 2012)

• Boswellia serrata:
RCTs demonstrate significant improvement in osteoarthritis pain and function (WOMAC scores).
(Kimmatkar et al., Phytomedicine, 2003)

• Berberine (from Berberis aristata):
Randomized trials show HbA1c reduction comparable to metformin in type 2 diabetes.
(Yin et al., Metabolism, 2008)

So the statement “Ayurveda has no high-quality evidence” is simply incorrect.

The honest scientific position is: evidence in Ayurveda is condition-specific and uneven, not absent. And that’s true for many areas of modern medicine too.

Also, let’s not pretend modern medicine has a definitive pharmacological cure for NAFLD — current management is still largely lifestyle-based.

If your standard is RCTs, apply it across the board — not selectively.

Ayurveda is a Scientific System with Strong Evidence Base
1️⃣ Ayurveda – A Systematic & Scientific Medical Science
Ayurveda is not merely a traditional belief system; it is a systematic, logical, and evidence-based medical science developed through:
Pratyakṣa (direct observation)
Anumāna (inference)
Āptopadeśa (authoritative testimony)
Yukti (rational application & experimentation)
These are classical scientific methods mentioned in Charaka Samhita, proving that Ayurveda follows structured reasoning and clinical validation.
2️⃣ Concept of Evidence in Ayurveda
In modern terms, evidence includes research trials, pharmacological studies, and clinical validation. Ayurveda already described:
Hetu (cause)
Lakṣaṇa (symptoms)
Upaśaya-Anupaśaya (therapeutic test)
Samprapti (pathogenesis)
This is similar to modern diagnostic methodology.
3️⃣ Modern Scientific Validation
Today, many Ayurvedic principles are supported by research:
Turmeric (Haridra) → Curcumin proven anti-inflammatory and antioxidant.
Ashwagandha → Clinically proven adaptogen reducing stress and cortisol.
Triphala → Research supports antioxidant & gut-regulating effects.
Panchakarma → Studies show detoxification, metabolic correction, and improved inflammatory markers.
Institutions like:
Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS)
All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA)
World Health Organization (WHO supports traditional medicine integration)
are actively conducting scientific trials and publishing evidence.
4️⃣ WHO Recognition
The World Health Organization has recognized traditional medicine systems and established the Global Centre for Traditional Medicine in India, showing global scientific interest in Ayurveda.
5️⃣ Personalized & Preventive Approach (Advanced Scientific Thinking)
Ayurveda introduced:
Prakriti-based personalization (similar to modern genetic individuality)
Preventive healthcare (Swasthavritta)
Lifestyle & diet regulation (Ahara-Vihara science)
Modern medicine is now adopting:
Personalized medicine
Preventive & lifestyle medicine
Gut-brain axis concepts
Ayurveda described these thousands of years ago.
6️⃣ Pharmacology & Pharmaceutics
Ayurveda has:
Detailed Dravyaguna Vigyana
Standardized pharmaceutical procedures (Bhavana, Shodhana, Marana)
Dose, Anupana, Kala, Matra concepts
These indicate a clear pharmacological framework.
🔎 Conclusion
Ayurveda is: ✔ Logical
✔ Experimental
✔ Evidence-based (classical + modern research)
✔ Globally recognized
✔ Scientifically structured
It is not merely faith-based; it is a holistic biomedical science validated through both classical pramāṇa and modern research methodologies.

comments.text:
You have dedicated yourself to defending that tradition. You have become one of its most articulate public ambassadors. Your scholarship is impressive, your arguments are meticulously researched, your presentations are lucid, and your calm, measured style has earned you a large and loyal audience. You possess something that very few doctors possess—the ability to explain complex medical science to ordinary people in language they can understand. For that, you deserve appreciation rather than criticism.

Yet admiration does not prevent one from making a humble request. My request is simply this: while defending science with all the passion at your command, please do not be so relentless in dismantling every alternative system of medicine that you unintentionally dismantle the dignity of the men and women who practise it.

There is a distinction between exposing falsehood and humiliating people. One is a scientific duty; the other is a human choice.

I often wonder whether you have paused to think about the audience watching your videos. Certainly there are patients. Certainly there are doctors. Certainly there are people who profit from misinformation. But there is another audience that remains invisible.

Across India, in hundreds of hostels, thousands of young students are studying Ayurveda, Homoeopathy, Unani and Siddha. Many of them did not arrive there because it was the fulfilment of a lifelong dream. Like millions of other young Indians, they dreamt of entering an MBBS programme. They worked hard, appeared for competitive examinations, and discovered, as countless others do every year, that our educational system is merciless in its selection. Their first choice slipped away. They accepted their second or third choice, not because they lacked intelligence or sincerity, but because life had closed one door and left another slightly open.

They picked themselves up. They entered their colleges. They lived in dingy hostel rooms. They memorised, studied, sat for examinations and spent five and a half years preparing themselves for a profession that they hoped would allow them to live with dignity and serve society.

Then they encounter your videos.

There appears before them a distinguished physician, scholarly, articulate, impeccably qualified, handsome with his characteristic salt-and-pepper beard, speaking flawless English with that gentle Malayalam cadence that has become instantly recognisable. Behind him stands a research team that combs through medical literature, producing paper after paper, trial after trial and fact after fact. One by one, the claims of alternative medicine are examined, challenged and often demolished.

For the scientifically trained viewer, it is an excellent exercise in critical thinking. For the young Ayurvedic student sitting alone in a hostel room, it can feel like something very different. It can feel as though the foundations of the life he is trying to build are being steadily pulled away beneath his feet.

There is something profoundly unequal about such an encounter. You have your qualifications, your platform, your command over scientific literature and the support of researchers who help you prepare your presentations. The young Homoeopathy student, the Ayurvedic intern or the Unani graduate has none of these advantages. They are not equipped to enter a public debate with you. They simply watch, absorb, and quietly wonder whether the profession to which they have devoted years of their youth deserves only ridicule. This constant ridicule may pile up and the young boy or girl may end up doing something irreversible. I shudder to even think about it. May God give them strength to bear the daily humiliations by you on social media.

Science has already established its supremacy where it matters most. Even many practitioners of AYUSH acknowledge this without hesitation. When they or their loved ones suffer a myocardial infarction, a stroke, overwhelming sepsis, diabetic ketoacidosis, major trauma or require complex surgery, they do exactly what everyone else does. They go to a modern hospital. When cancer requires chemotherapy, radiotherapy or surgery, they seek the expertise of oncologists. They know the difference between tradition and evidence. They know which system has transformed survival through rigorous science.

Modern medicine, therefore, has nothing to fear from AYUSH. It has already won the argument. That is precisely why I appeal to your generosity.

There is another reality that perhaps deserves equal consideration. Every doctor has, at some point, looked into the eyes of a family and uttered the most painful sentence medicine can produce: "We have done everything we can. Please take your loved one home."

Imagine a daughter bringing home her mother with end-stage metastatic cancer after every evidence-based option has been exhausted. Surgery has been performed where possible. Chemotherapy has run its course. Radiotherapy has been given. The specialists have done everything that present-day medical science could reasonably offer. The prognosis is measured not in years but in weeks.

What does that daughter do the following morning? Does she simply sit beside the bed waiting for death?

Or does she search for something—anything—that allows her to feel that she is still caring for the person who gave her life?

A Homoeopathy friend brings a small box of sweet homoeopathic pills worth the cost of a pizza. A relative recommends an Ayurvedic preparation. Another friend suggests a traditional ritualistic remedy. None of these should ever replace treatments of proven benefit while such treatments remain available, and no honest practitioner should promise miracles where science has found none. But once medicine itself has acknowledged that curative options have been exhausted, families often seek something that offers emotional participation in the final journey.

Perhaps what follows is simply the placebo effect. If so, the placebo effect itself is a remarkable expression of the human mind's capacity to influence the experience of illness. Perhaps the disease follows its own natural course and there is an unexpected period of stability or spontaneous remission that medicine itself cannot confidently attribute to the remedy being taken. A rare co-incidence. Strictly speaking, science may not agree with that conclusion. Yet I ask myself a different question. At that stage, when hospitals have already said, "There is nothing more we can do," is our first moral duty to correct the family's attribution, or is it to recognise that what they are really holding on to is not a pharmacological mechanism but hope, love, participation and the comforting belief that they did not stop caring until the very last moment?

If no proven treatment has been denied, if no patient has been diverted away from life-saving care, and if a grieving family finds consolation in believing that they continued to do something meaningful for someone they loved, perhaps compassion allows us to leave that fragile comfort undisturbed. There are moments in life when winning an argument is less important than preserving a human heart , to mourn for the loss of a loved one fighting a terminal disease.

Please do not misunderstand me. I am not defending deception. I am not defending those who exploit vulnerable patients by making extravagant claims or persuading them to abandon effective treatment. Such people deserve exposure, criticism and, where appropriate, legal action. They bring disrepute not only to modern medicine but also to sincere practitioners within AYUSH itself.

My plea is for —the ordinary Ayurvedacharya, the Homoeopath in a small town, the Unani physician serving a rural community, the Siddha practitioner who genuinely wishes to reduce suffering within the limits of his traditional knowledge. They may not possess your brilliant scientific training, high grades and gift of the gab or your high qualifications or your huge funds and backup research team or affiliation to a multibillion medical practice. They may never publish in prestigious journals. They may even privately acknowledge that modern medicine stands on firmer scientific ground. Yet they too are human beings trying to find meaning, dignity and purpose in the profession that life placed before them.

May I also respectfully mention one issue that repeatedly surfaces in public discussions—the prefix "Dr." I understand the legal and academic complexities surrounding it. I understand your concern that the public should never be misled about qualifications. Transparency is essential. But I also request that you consider the emotional impact of repeatedly casting aspersions on that prefix when used by AYUSH graduates who have earned degrees recognised under the laws of this country. Every time the prefix itself becomes an object of ridicule, thousands of sincere graduates hear not merely a legal argument but a message that their years of study count for nothing and that even the identity they earned deserves public contempt.

Surely there is a way of protecting the public without diminishing the dignity of an entire community.

The hallmark of great science is not merely that it is correct. It is that it remains humane even when it is correct.
